record.title: Google DeepMind reports AI-assisted machine-checked proofs for selected Signal protocol code properties
record.summary: Google DeepMind’s Nov 10 paper and public Lean repository report machine-checked symbolic and computational proofs for selected security properties of compiled AArch64 `libsignal` code in a CLI harness. The proofs concern the PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet and reportedly establish properties including forward secrecy, post-compromise security, authentication and confidentiality under the paper’s specifications. Human-guided specification and hooked primitive contracts are part of the proof boundary. The paper reports proof teams typically had 40–80 agents working on one machine for 24–72 hours; the public README says a clean full proof build takes several hours and peaks at about 15–34 GiB RAM. These figures describe proof campaigns and a verification build, not total project cost, human effort or demonstrated scalable economics. The work does not cover Signal’s mobile apps or server/group protocols, and the computational theorem has explicit cryptographic assumptions and attacker/model restrictions. WIRED notes prior Signal formal-verification work provided a head start. the research desk inspected the paper and repository page but did not build or independently replay the proofs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The official paper reports that a human-guided multi-agent framework produced Lean-kernel-checked symbolic and computational proofs for selected security properties of compiled AArch64 `libsignal` code in a CLI harness. Reported scope includes the PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet; the specification, environment contracts and cryptographic assumptions define what the theorems cover.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that two previously fixed `libsignal` bugs were reintroduced and that Lean proofs showed the resulting binaries violated the stated symbolic security theorems.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Google DeepMind published a dated technical paper and an accessible public Lean proof repository on November 10, 2026.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected sources do not establish independent reproduction, verification of Signal’s mobile applications or server/group protocols, measured project cost, or scalable production adoption. The computational proof has explicit cryptographic assumptions and a restricted adversary/environment model; the paper’s symbolic result addresses only part of the post-quantum gap.

evidence_gaps.description: The official repository is public, but its exact commit and dependencies were not pinned and the Lean proof build was not replayed in this activation.
No independent formal-methods review of the specifications, contracts, trusted computing base or proof coverage was inspected.
The inspected sources do not quantify compute, person-hours, expert review effort or matched cost versus earlier Signal verification work.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported workflow generalizes, it could make machine-checked verification of high-impact software implementations more tractable and change how security assurance is produced. The evidence currently concerns one human-guided proof-of-concept, not verification of all Signal software or demonstrated scalable economics.
limitations: The technical result is reported in an official paper and public proof repository; the research desk did not pin the repository to a commit, build it, or independently replay the Lean proofs.
The proofs cover compiled AArch64 code from a `libsignal` CLI harness, not Signal mobile applications, server components, group messaging or all protocol behavior.

The proof depends on a trusted specification and on contracts for hooked routines and cryptographic primitives; the paper identifies the AArch64/Linux semantics, build tooling and definitions as part of its trusted base.

The computational proof makes cryptographic assumptions and uses a restricted attacker/environment model; the paper states it gives no guarantee against a quantum adversary, while the symbolic proof covers only part of that gap.
The paper models one session per handshake, fixed message lengths and no multi-device state, among other stated limitations.
No measured cost or matched human-effort comparison was published in the inspected sources; WIRED reports prior Signal formal-verification work provided a head start.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports Lean-kernel-checked symbolic and computational security proofs for selected properties of compiled AArch64 `libsignal` CLI-harness code, and reports detection of two reintroduced historical bugs.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports proof campaigns typically used 40–80 agents on a single machine for 24–72 hours. The public README states a clean build of all proofs takes several hours and about 15–34 GiB peak RAM. These are source-reported compute/parallelism figures; total project compute cost, human effort, and a matched cost comparison are not quantified.
technical.demonstrated_result: The dated full paper and public Apache-2.0 proof repository were inspected. The existence and contents of the reported proof artifact are observable; proof validity, build reproducibility and theorem adequacy were not independently verified in this activation.
technical.implementation_status: Official paper and Lean proof repository are public under Apache-2.0; no independent build/replay or production adoption was verified.
technical.mechanism: A human-guided specification agent and reviewer agents produce Lean theorem statements; autonomous prover agents generate proofs checked by Lean. The code is compiled to AArch64 and modeled with formal machine-code/Linux semantics. Hooked low-level cryptographic routines are represented by contracts.
technical.novelty: The authors report protocol-level security proofs connected to unmodified compiled code of a widely deployed cryptographic protocol implementation, extending beyond abstract protocol models and verification-friendly reimplementations.
technical.regime: Compiled AArch64 `libsignal` reference implementation in a CLI harness, selected one-to-one protocol sessions, fixed-length messages, no multi-device state, and explicit cryptographic, environment and attacker assumptions.
technical.reproducibility: The public repository documents pinned Lean/Rust toolchains, proof build commands and comparator checks. the research desk inspected these instructions but did not resolve and run them; independent replay remains open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Prior Signal formal verification and cryptographic-protocol proofs are discussed in the paper; WIRED reports this prior work provided a head start. No matched time/cost baseline was available.

brief.title: Google DeepMind reports AI-assisted machine-checked proofs for selected Signal protocol code properties
brief.why_it_matters: Machine-checked security proofs for selected properties of compiled production-library code could shift assurance from finding bugs toward proving specified properties. The result is a substantial but bounded case: its proof boundary depends on human-reviewed specifications, contracts and model assumptions, and it does not establish the security of Signal applications as deployed.
